To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the effectiveness of any heat mitigation policy depends on the following factors: 1) the specific location of the heat island, and its proximity to other urban areas; 2) the time of day, day of year, and year of implementation; and 3) the type and intensity of the heat mitigation policy.

(1) the urban environment is an archipelago of interacting urban areas, each of which has a distinct climate, (2) the urban environment has a complex, three-dimensional structure, (3) the urban environment varies in time, (4) urban heat mitigation policy should focus on the health of people, not air temperatures, and (5) policy should be based on a scientific understanding of the urban environment.

(1) urban areas are complex systems with multiple interacting components; (2) the urban heat island effect is a result of the interaction of multiple meteorological processes; (3) the urban heat mitigation policy and planning process should be informed by an understanding of the spatial, temporal, and meteorological complexities of the urban heat island; and (4) the ultimate goal of heat mitigation policies is to reduce heat-related morbidity and mortality, and therefore should be designed to do so.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how to improve the effectiveness of heat-related policy and planning by better integrating scientific understanding into the process.
how to improve urban heat mitigation policies, with the ultimate goal of reducing the negative impacts of urban heat on human health and well-being.
the science of heat mitigation, and its application to policy-making.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the urban heat island effect is real and can be mitigated by a variety of approaches.

the most effective way to improve heat-related health outcomes in urban environments is to develop a comprehensive understanding of the urban heat mitigation problem, and then use that knowledge to develop and implement location-specific policies and programs that address the specific needs of the area in question.

urban heat mitigation strategies must be based on an integrated understanding of the urban environment, including the interactions between urban and natural environments, and that the ultimate goal of such policies is to improve human health outcomes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the most effective policies are those that recognize the importance of the spatial and temporal scales of urban heat, and that incorporate the full range of atmospheric parameters that influence human health outcomes.
we are able to provide a scientific basis for urban planning and policy to reduce heat related health outcomes.

urban heat mitigation policies should be based on an in-depth understanding of how meteorological parameters, both within the urban environment and at its edges, interact to produce the heat-related health outcomes that the policy is intended to mitigate.
The main takeaway from our work is that

urban heat mitigation strategies must consider the full range of spatial, temporal, and human health-related considerations, and that this requires a close collaboration between the scientific community and policy-makers.

the urban heat island problem is a complex, multi-scale problem that requires a multi-scale approach to its solution, and that this approach needs to be integrated with the actual end-point goal, namely, human health.
the design, implementation, and assessment of urban heat mitigation strategies should not be done in isolation.
